title: This space company is betting its future on a propellant available everywhere
gist: Argo Space, founded by three former SpaceX engineers, is building water-propelled spacecraft that split water into hydrogen and oxygen with solar power, aiming for a logistics network spanning LEO, GEO and the Moon. Its first Navigator demo could not test propulsion. Two 2027 Chiron missions for a national-security customer will fly on non-SpaceX rockets because Falcon 9 rideshare slots are scarce.

insights.claim: Argo Space was founded in late 2022 to build in-space infrastructure using water, which may be harvestable on the Moon and is found throughout the Solar System, so spacecraft would not depend on propellant launched from Earth.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: In-situ resource use is a bet on the long-term structure of the cislunar economy.
insights.quote: We based the company on water

insights.claim: Robert Carlisle argues that water-based transportation will create a profit motive to harvest water from the Moon's shallower gravity well.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Demand for propellant could make lunar mining commercially viable.

insights.claim: Water also serves as coolant and radiation shield for thrusters and avionics, which increases propellant mass fraction so the vehicle can travel farther.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Using water for several jobs on board is a design advantage behind the claimed performance.
insights.locator: The availability of water is key

insights.claim: Chiron launches with liquid water, splits it into hydrogen and oxygen gas in space using solar power, and burns them in a conventional rocket engine. This gives more thrust than ion thrusters at similar power and avoids cryogenic storage.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: It is a technical path distinct from electric propulsion, with a different tradeoff between thrust and complexity.

insights.claim: NASA demonstrated water propulsion on two small satellites in late 2017, and Momentus has used water propellant, but Argo aims to do it at larger scale.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Argo is not the only water-propulsion player, so its differentiation rests on scale.

insights.claim: Argo claims more than 2 km/s of delta-v in a roughly 200 kg Chiron spacecraft, enough to raise a 400 km circular orbit to more than 5,000 km or to provide several decades of geostationary station-keeping.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: If the performance holds, it supports satellite life-extension and repositioning services.
insights.locator: Argo says it can achieve more

insights.claim: Argonaut, Argo's follow-on vehicle, targets a maximum payload of 1,400 kg and a maximum delta-v of 17 km/s per tank. In September, ispace signed to have Argonaut deliver its Lunar Connect relay satellite to lunar orbit later this decade.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: An early commercial lunar customer validates demand for cislunar transport.
insights.locator: But Argo is aiming to do

insights.claim: Two Chiron missions in 2027 will carry payloads for an undisclosed national-security customer, one to LEO and one to geostationary transfer orbit, to demonstrate propulsion and maneuvering between orbits.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: National-security demand is anchoring early in-space mobility startups.
insights.locator: The company plans two Chiron missions

insights.claim: The July Navigator demo on a Falcon 9 rideshare validated flight software, avionics and structures, but one of two solar arrays failed to deploy, leaving the craft power-negative with no propulsion test.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The core technology is still unproven in flight, which is the main execution risk.
insights.locator: Argo Space flew its first demonstration

insights.claim: SpaceX is pulling back on the commercial availability of Falcon 9, so neither Chiron mission will fly on a SpaceX vehicle. One flies on an undisclosed new commercial rocket, which is a calculated risk, and the other on a government-furnished launcher.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Tight Falcon 9 rideshare capacity creates openings for new launch providers and adds schedule risk for small-satellite companies.
insights.locator: It’s notable that the Carlisles spent

insights.claim: Robert Carlisle says Falcon 9 rides require a waitlist stretching a year and a half to two years or more, with no launches available for sale.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Launch supply constraints are a binding bottleneck across the space economy.
insights.quote: There’s not launches available for sale.

insights.claim: Argo has raised $20 million to date with fewer than 30 people, and Kirby Carlisle argues spacecraft need far less capital than rockets because they do not need heavy ground infrastructure such as SpaceX's McGregor test site.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Spacecraft startups can reach milestones with much less funding than launch companies, which affects venture return profiles.
insights.quote: We don’t need a McGregor, right?

insights.claim: The Carlisle brothers launched, refurbished and sold Falcon 9 rockets at SpaceX, but chose to build spacecraft rather than rockets for their own company.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Insiders see more opportunity in in-space infrastructure than in competing on launch.
